prompt: A sunflower seed with a mass of less than 1 gram was planted in a pot of soil. Months later, the plant had a mass of about 2,000 grams, but the mass of the soil had barely changed. Where did most of the plant's added mass come from?
explanation: Plants build their bodies mostly from carbon dioxide taken from the air and water taken in by the roots. Sunlight supplies the energy for this, not the matter. That is why the plant gained about 2,000 grams while the soil lost almost nothing.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: light is a material that becomes part of the plant; light supplies energy, not mass.
misconception: fertilizer is plant food that builds most of the plant; it adds only small amounts of minerals.
misconception: plants get their mass from the soil; the soil mass barely changed while the plant gained about 2,000 grams.

real_world_check: Plants get the materials they need for growth chiefly from air (carbon dioxide) and water, not from the soil (NGSS 5-LS1-1).

prompt: Suppose every worm, fungus, and bacterium living in a forest's soil were removed, and none came back. Which prediction about the forest over the next several years is most likely correct?
choices: Plants would grow larger, since soil life would stop taking food from their roots.
Dead leaves would break down faster, because sunlight would turn them into soil.
Dead leaves would pile up, and plants would get fewer nutrients.
Deer would begin to make their own food from sunlight.
correct_answer: Dead leaves would pile up, and plants would get fewer nutrients.
explanation: Worms, fungi, and bacteria are decomposers. They break down dead leaves and return nutrients to the soil, where plant roots take them up. Without decomposers, dead matter would build up and the soil would run short of nutrients for plants.

distractor_rationales.choice: Plants would grow larger, since soil life would stop taking food from their roots.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: decomposers compete with plants for food; they actually return the nutrients plants need, so plants would do worse.

distractor_rationales.choice: Dead leaves would break down faster, because sunlight would turn them into soil.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: rotting is caused by sunlight; dead matter is broken down mainly by living decomposers, so it would break down more slowly.

distractor_rationales.choice: Deer would begin to make their own food from sunlight.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: animals can switch to making food; only producers such as plants make food from sunlight.

real_world_check: Decomposers break down dead organisms and return their matter to the soil, where plants reuse it; without them, dead matter builds up and nutrients stop cycling.

prompt: In a field, deer eat thistle plants. Some thistles have longer spines than others, and deer eat these less often. These plants make more seeds, which grow into plants with long spines. No new thistles come in from outside the field. After many years, most thistles in the field have long spines. What process is this?
explanation: Thistles already varied in spine length. Long-spined plants were eaten less, so they made more seeds and passed long spines to their young. Over many generations the long-spined kind became most common. That is natural selection.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: plants learn to grow longer spines during their lives and pass that on; spine length is inherited from parents, not learned.
misconception: a population changes because new organisms move in; the scenario says no new thistles came in from outside.
misconception: a population changes form the way one insect changes in its life cycle; metamorphosis happens to one animal, not across generations of plants.

real_world_check: Differences among individuals of a species can give advantages in surviving and reproducing, so over generations the helpful trait becomes more common (natural selection).

real_world_check: Decomposers such as molds and bacteria break down dead plant and animal matter and return it to the soil, where plants can use it again.

prompt: A sealed glass jar holds soil, water, moss, small snails, and tiny decomposers. It sits by a sunny window. Years later, the moss and snails are still alive, though no food has been added. Which statement best explains how they keep surviving?
choices: The snails make their own food from sunlight, so they do not need the moss.
The moss takes its food from the soil, which holds enough food to last for years.
Snails eat the moss, and decomposers turn wastes into nutrients the moss uses again.
The moss and snails live off food packed into the jar at the start, which is running out.
correct_answer: Snails eat the moss, and decomposers turn wastes into nutrients the moss uses again.
explanation: Matter cycles inside the jar. The moss makes food from light, air, and water; the snails eat the moss; decomposers break down wastes and dead matter into nutrients that the moss takes up again. Because the same matter is reused, no food has to be added.

distractor_rationales.choice: The snails make their own food from sunlight, so they do not need the moss.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: animals can make food from sunlight; only producers such as moss do.

distractor_rationales.choice: The moss takes its food from the soil, which holds enough food to last for years.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: plants take in food from the soil; moss makes its own food from light, air, and water.

distractor_rationales.choice: The moss and snails live off food packed into the jar at the start, which is running out.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: living things use up a one-time store of matter; a stored supply would have run out, while cycling lets the jar last for years.

real_world_check: In an ecosystem, matter cycles among plants, animals, and decomposers: producers make food, consumers eat them, and decomposers return nutrients to the soil.

prompt: On a dark night, an owl catches a mouse that it cannot see clearly. The mouse is moving through dry leaves. Which statement best explains how the owl finds the mouse?
choices: Its eyes send out beams of light that bounce off the mouse and show where it is.
Its ears pick up the rustling sound, and its brain uses those signals to tell where the mouse is.
It hears the mouse, and its ears decide on their own which way to fly.
It remembers where mice were the night before, so it does not need its senses.
correct_answer: Its ears pick up the rustling sound, and its brain uses those signals to tell where the mouse is.
explanation: The moving mouse makes sound in the dry leaves. The owl's ears take in that sound and send signals to its brain, and the brain uses them to work out where the mouse is so the owl can strike.

distractor_rationales.choice: Its eyes send out beams of light that bounce off the mouse and show where it is.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: eyes give off light to see; eyes only take in light that enters them.

distractor_rationales.choice: It hears the mouse, and its ears decide on their own which way to fly.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: sense organs make decisions by themselves; ears only send signals, and the brain processes them and decides.

distractor_rationales.choice: It remembers where mice were the night before, so it does not need its senses.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: animals can find moving prey without sensing it; mice move, so the owl needs current sense information.

real_world_check: Animals take in information through sense organs such as ears, which send signals to the brain, where the information is processed to guide actions (NGSS 4-LS1-2).

prompt: In a field, grasshoppers of one kind are either green or tan. Birds eat the grasshoppers they spot most easily. A long dry spell turns the grass tan for many years. Grasshoppers pass their color to their young. What will most likely happen to the grasshoppers in the field over many generations?
choices: More of them will be tan, because birds spot and eat tan ones less often.
Green ones will turn their bodies tan so birds will not see them.
Tan ones will die out, because green ones feed better in dry grass.
The mix of colors will stay as it was, since birds catch both colors equally often.
correct_answer: More of them will be tan, because birds spot and eat tan ones less often.
explanation: On tan grass, tan grasshoppers are harder for birds to spot, so more of them live long enough to have young. Because color is passed to the young, the share of tan grasshoppers grows over many generations.

distractor_rationales.choice: Green ones will turn their bodies tan so birds will not see them.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: individuals change their inherited traits because they need to; a grasshopper cannot change its color to match, and change happens across generations.

distractor_rationales.choice: Tan ones will die out, because green ones feed better in dry grass.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the color that matches the background is the one that loses; tan ones are hidden on tan grass, and color does not decide which grasshoppers find food.

distractor_rationales.choice: The mix of colors will stay as it was, since birds catch both colors equally often.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: predators catch every color equally; the scenario says birds eat the ones they spot most easily.

real_world_check: When individuals vary in an inherited trait that affects survival, such as color against a background, the helpful variation becomes more common over generations.
